claims.text: Haryana's Department of Art and Cultural Affairs calls India's stone-carving tradition one of the richest in the world.

quotes.quote: The stone-carving tradition in India is one of the richest in the world.

claims.text: The classical tradition of Indian stone carving was closely linked with architecture, as the carvings of major temples such as Puri and Khajuraho illustrate.

quotes.quote: The classical tradition of stone carving was closely linked with architecture. All major temples of India-be it Puri, Konark, Khajuraho, Kailash Temple, or the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram-illustrate the rich tradition of Indian stone carvings.

claims.text: Stone carving in general is a conservative craft; there are only a limited number of ways to shape stone, and techniques are broadly similar worldwide.

quotes.quote: Stone carving is generally a conservative craft. There are only a limited number of ways to shape stone and broad similarities in technique can be noted all around the world and throughout history.

claims.text: Rajasthan continues to be one of the major centres of stone carving in India, according to Haryana's culture department.

quotes.quote: Rajasthan continues to be one of major centres of stone carving in the country.

claims.text: The tooth chisel, often used in marble carving and with a long history around the Aegean and Italy, is almost entirely absent from Pakistan and India, where granite, sandstone and schist are the dominant stones.

quotes.quote: The tooth chisel, therefore, a tool often used in marble carving, has a long history around the Aegean and Italy, areas rich in marble, but is almost entirely absent from Pakistan and India, where granite, sandstone and schist are the dominant stones.

claims.text: Guilds of masons and stone carvers have existed in India since the 7th century BC, according to Haryana's culture department.

quotes.quote: Guilds of masons and stone carvers have existed here since the 7th century B.C.

claims.text: Stone-carving skills were handed down as family lore from father to son, a practice still prevalent in some parts of India.

quotes.quote: The skills were handed down as family lore from father to son, a practise prevalent in some parts of the country even today.

claims.text: From medieval times the ready availability of high-quality stone, with brick almost unknown, let Rajasthani builders raise strong forts, palaces and temples.

quotes.quote: Right from the medieval times, the ready availability of high-quality stone (the use of brick was almost unknown) made it easy for the Rajasthani builder to construct strong and beautiful forts, palaces, and temples.

claims.text: Stone carving is a very ancient tradition in Bihar, and it reached its zenith there during the Mauryan period.

quotes.quote: Stone carving is a very ancient tradition in Bihar. The craft achieved its zenith during the Mauryan period

claims.text: The finest examples of Bihar's Mauryan stone carving are the rock-cut caves of the Barabar and Nagarjuni Hills in Jahanabad district.

quotes.quote: its finest examples are the rock-cut caves of Barabar and Nagarjuni Hills in Jahanabad District.

claims.text: Two stone-carving traditions emerged in Gujarat, one based on the Shilpa Shastras and the other on village traditions.

quotes.quote: In Gujarat, two stone carving traditions emerged, one based on the Shilpa Shastras (the sacred guidelines for art and architecture) and the other on village traditions.

claims.text: India Currents writes that Gujarat's stonework evolved dramatically under Solanki rule (942-1304) and during the Sultanate reign (1403-1573).

quotes.quote: The tradition of stonework in Gujarat evolved dramatically during two major periods: under Solanki rule (942-1304) and during the Sultanate reign (1403-1573).

claims.text: In Solanki-period Gujarat, Jain temples were distinguished from Hindu temples by heavy use of marble, against the limestone and sandstone prevalent in Hindu temples.

quotes.quote: During the Solanki rule, Hindu and Jain temples were architecturally similar.
The significant difference is the heavy use of marble in Jain temples, in contrast to the limestone and sandstone prevalent in Hindu temples.

claims.text: Gujarat's Sultanate rulers built mosques and tombs on Islamic principles but engaged local stone craftsmen, long masters of Hindu and Jain temple architecture, for the embellishments.

quotes.quote: The rules commissioned mosques and tombs according to traditional Islamic principles. However, they engaged the local stone craftsmen, longtime masters of Hindu and Jain temple architecture, for the embellishments.

claims.text: Most structures built in Gujarat during the Solanki period had their stone blocks fitted without mortar.

quotes.quote: As with most structures built during the Solanki period, the stone blocks were fitted without mortar.

claims.text: Jha's Dhakotha study, conducted in 2010-2011, describes soapstone carving there as a comparatively new craft with around 55-60 years of existence.

quotes.quote: Soapstone carving is respectively a newer soapstone craft in Dhakotha area with around 55-60 year's existence in this area.
This craft study cum design intervention initiative was conducted during 2010-2011 by this author.

claims.text: Folkartopedia, citing UMSAS, writes that some 400 years ago 1300 Gaud Brahmins built the Vishnupad Temple and most of their families stayed on.

quotes.quote: Some 400 years ago, the 1300 Gaud Brahmins built the famous Vishnupadh Temple. Most of the families stayed back and continued the sculpture making from local stones.

claims.text: The Free Press Journal writes that in 1787 Queen Ahilyabai Holkar brought skilled craftsmen from Rajasthan to Gaya to build the Vishnupad temple.

quotes.quote: In 1787, Queen Ahilyabai Holkar brought skilled craftsmen from Rajasthan to Gaya, Bihar to construct the historic Vishnupad temple.
the stone carvers, who came from Rajasthan to Bihar in the 18th century, brought to the state.

claims.text: The Free Press Journal calls Pattharkatti carving a 300-year-old craft reportedly promoted in the area by Queen Ahilyabai Holkar.

quotes.quote: The traditional carving is a 300-year-old traditional craft was reportedly promoted in the area by Queen Ahilyabai Holkar, who discovered black granite hills while travelling.

claims.text: The director of UMSAS told The Better India that black-stone sculptures across Bihar, especially in Nalanda district, are much older than the Vishnupada temple, and that such stones are found only in Patharkatti.

quotes.quote: We have found several sculptures made from black stone across Bihar, especially in the Nalanda district, which are much older than the Vishnupada temple.
Such stones are only found in Patharkatti village, and some settlements were living in the area before communities from Rajasthan came in

claims.text: Stone carving at Patharkatti was traditionally limited to Gaud Brahmins who migrated from Rajasthan at the invitation of Rani Ahilyabai of Indore.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, the work was limited to the Gaud Brahmins who migrated from Rajasthan on the invitation of Rani Ahilyabai of Indore.

claims.text: In the 1960s Upendra Maharathi Shilp Anusandhan Sansthan started a training centre at Patharkatti to bring people from other communities into the craft.

quotes.quote: This craft was limited to the Gaud Brahmins till recently when in the 1960s Upendra Maharathi Shilp Anusandhan Sansthan started a training center to involve people from other communities.
The most recent attempt was made in the 1960s by UMSAS.

claims.text: According to folklore recounted by The Better India, the Maharaja of Tekari allotted the temple workers land in Patharkatti village, 40 kilometres from Gaya, where they could at first quarry stone for free.

quotes.quote: According to folklore, she was searching for craftsmen to erect the temple with stones that could survive harsh weather conditions.
On the completion of the structure, when the workers wanted to return home, the Maharaja of Tekari allotted them a piece of land in Patharkatti village, 40 kilometres away from Gaya.
Since the area fell under the Maharaja's jurisdiction, the artisans were allowed to quarry the stone for free initially, and later at an annual royalty of Rs 1.50.

claims.text: In a master builder's account published by Himalayan Academy, shilpis, sculptors, and sthapatis, sculptor-architect-builders, worked for millennia in tightly organised guilds.

quotes.quote: Here one master builder, V. Ganapati Sthapati speaks of his mystical craft.
For millennia, shilpis (sculptors) and sthapatis (sculptor-architect-builders) worked in tightly-organized guilds.

claims.text: In the guild tradition a master sthapati describes, training was hereditary, began formally at age 12 in the workshop and took no less than 10 years.

quotes.quote: Training was hereditary, from father to son, and started formally at the age 12. Students were given practical training, not in a separate college, but right in the workshop
A complete training extended for not less than 10 years.

claims.text: In the sthapati tradition, one who works on architectural stones is called a takshaka and one who works on sculptural pieces a shilpi.

quotes.quote: One who works on architectural stones is called a takshaka, and one who works on a sculptural pieces is technically called a shilpi.

claims.text: Stone artisans of the Sompura community trace their origins to Aparajita, son of Vishwakarma, the architect of heaven.

quotes.quote: Stone artisans from the Sompura community trace their origins to Aparajita, the son of heaven's architect, Vishwakarma.

claims.text: In stone carving generally, Rockwell calls the point chisel the workhorse of carving, cutting away at least 85% of the stone removed in carving a statue.

quotes.quote: This chisel is the workhorse of carving. At least 85% of the stone removed in the process of carving a statue is cut away using this tool.

claims.text: The Art of Making in Antiquity essay says the point tends to be held perpendicular to granite and other hard stones, shattering the surface, since at a shallower angle it would bounce off.

quotes.quote: On granite and other hard stones it tends to be held perpendicular to the surface of the stone; a stroke at this angle effectively shatters the surface of the stone. At a shallower angle the chisel would simply bounce off these hard materials.

claims.text: The Art of Making in Antiquity essay says metal carving tools need continual sharpening, and that in India teams of twenty carvers are routinely accompanied by as many as three blacksmiths.

quotes.quote: Since metal carving tools also need continual sharpening, blacksmiths and carvers have always had a very close relationship.
In India, teams of twenty carvers are routinely accompanied by as many as three blacksmiths.

claims.text: The Art of Making in Antiquity essay says granite carvers in India still use the same basic range of tools as their predecessors centuries earlier.

quotes.quote: Granite carvers in India and marble carvers in Italy still use the same basic range of tools as their predecessors centuries earlier.

claims.text: Across stone-carving traditions, the electric saw, drill, angle grinder and air hammer were relatively late twentieth-century introductions that are still only used sparsely.

quotes.quote: even mechanized tools -such as the electric saw, drill, angle grinder and air hammer- were relatively late, twentieth-century introductions which are still only used sparsely.

claims.text: In stone carving generally, abrasives from coarse emery to softer sandstone or pumice can be rubbed over the stone with water for a very smooth finish, the water removing the stone dust.

quotes.quote: For achieving a very smooth finish on stone, various kinds of abrasive materials can be rubbed across the surface.

These range from relatively coarse materials, like emery, to softer ones, such as sandstone or pumice. These materials are applied to the surface of the stone with water which helps to remove the stone dust created during the abrading process.

claims.text: In stone carving generally, a carver reaches a high polish by working from the rougher abrasives through to the finer ones, applying each in turn.

quotes.quote: In order to achieve a high level of polish the carver will work from the rougher abrasives through to the finer ones, applying each in turn.

claims.text: A high level of polish can only be achieved on certain stones, such as marble, granite or certain hard limestones.

quotes.quote: A high level of polish can only be achieved on certain types of stone, such as marble, granite or certain hard limestones.

claims.text: The Art of Making in Antiquity essay says saw blades for soft limestone, sandstone or tuff tend to be toothed, while on harder stones a flat blade is used with abrasives mixed in water.

quotes.quote: Smaller saws could have been operated by a single worker but only when they were used on soft limestone, sandstone or tuff. On these soft stones the blade tends to be toothed while on harder stones it is flat and used in conjunction with abrasives mixed in water.

claims.text: The Art of Making in Antiquity essay says carvers use the rasp mainly on marble, since it would have little effect on granite, while scrapers are easier for smoothing softer stones.

quotes.quote: It is mainly used by carvers on marble since it would have little effect on granite, while scrapers are easier to use for smoothing softer stones.

claims.text: The Art of Making in Antiquity essay says wooden wedges set in holes and soaked in water swell and force the stone to split along its natural bedding lines or faults.

quotes.quote: Wooden wedges are obviously too weak to break the stone directly and are instead inserted into rectangular holes, usually carved with the point, and then soaked in water. As the wood becomes saturated it expands and forces the stone to split along its natural bedding lines or faults.

claims.text: Jaisalmer's sandstone is extracted and broken with heavy machinery, and iron wedges are hammered into the rock to help cut it.

quotes.quote: Heavy machinery is required to extract and break the rock.
Iron wedges are hammered into the rock to facilitate its cutting.

claims.text: In Jaisalmer's stone factories, water on the giant hydraulic cutting blade softens the rock and cools it against the heat of cutting.

quotes.quote: The giant hydraulic blade used for cutting the rock. Water is used to soften the rock and to cool it, countering the heat produced in the cutting process.

claims.text: Jaisalmer artisans carve with small hand-held tools, mainly a hammer and chisels of different widths, the chisels diamond tipped for a hard, clean-cutting edge.

quotes.quote: the stone will be carved using small hand-held tools, primarily a hammer and chisels of different widths.
The chisels are diamond tipped, to give them a hard edge for clean cutting.

claims.text: In Jaisalmer a design traced on butter paper is laid on the slab as a guide, while for geometric designs the craftsperson generally draws a grid directly on the slab.

quotes.quote: A tracing of the design is made out on butter paper, and placed on the stone slab to be carved. This acts as a guide for the artisan to mark out the basic form of the design.
In the case of geometrical designs the craft person generally draws a grid directly on the slab.

claims.text: On Jaisalmer's carved panels the form is often cut with an electric tool, while the finer detailing is executed with a chisel.

quotes.quote: Often the form is carved with an electric tool, while the finer detailing is executed using a chisel.

claims.text: Dhakotha's soapstone carving is a phase-wise process shown in 12 stages, lettered A to L, ending in the final products.

quotes.quote: As illustrated in figure-8, different phase wise craftsmanship process is displayed in a number of 12 different stages; these stages are marked in this figure, as- 8(A) to 8(L).
6.2.2.2.1.1. Stage-A: Raw soapstone
Stage-L: Final products. [Process concluded]

claims.text: In stage B, primary stone cutting with chisel and hammer gives a semi-finished block that is ready for further work.

quotes.quote: Stage-B: Primary stone cutting with the help of chisel and hammer. This phase provides a semi-finished stone block, which is ready for further craftsmanship processes.

claims.text: Dhakotha carvers then cut the edges with a hand-operated electric stone cutter to get a uniformly surfaced block.

quotes.quote: Stage-C: Edge cutting with the help of hand operated electricity stone cutter to receive a uniformly surfaced stone block.

claims.text: A conceptual line drawing is made on plain paper, and the finalised drawing is drawn on the block with erasable HB pencils.

quotes.quote: Stage-E: Conceptual line-drawing on plain paper.
Stage-F: Finalized drawing gets drawn over the stone block received from 'Stage-D', with the help of erasable pencils, i.e., HB pencil.

claims.text: Because pencil marks might rub off during chiselling, carvers turn the drawn lines into lines etched in the surface with a fine-tipped chisel.

quotes.quote: As the HB pencil marks might erase during the soapstone chiseling process, so, craftsmen convert, final pencil drawn line marks, into the surface-etched line marks, with the help of a fine tipped chisel.

claims.text: Chiselling of the soapstone follows, and fine carving is then done with fine chisels.

quotes.quote: Stage-H: Chiseling process under progression.
Stage-J: Fine carving under progression, with the help of fine chisels.

claims.text: Sandpaper is applied over the chiselled soapstone surface to achieve the final finish.

quotes.quote: Stage-K: Application of sand paper over a chiseled surface, to achieve final finishing.

claims.text: Dhakotha's soapstone carvers commonly use chisel, hammer, mallet, a Lakdi Pidha support and a Jute Chatti cushion, with chisels in many cutting-tip shapes.

quotes.quote: Among tools- chisel, hammer, mallet, Lakdi Pidha, Jute Chatti etc. are commonly used by craftsmen for carving soapstone statues and other carved products.
Carves soapstone. Available with different cutting-tip variations

claims.text: The Jute Chatti cushions half-made soapstone pieces and prevents sharp-edged chipping, since soapstone is a soft stone.

quotes.quote: Jute Chatti Provide cushioning to half-made stone products, during further craftsmanship processes and prevent sharp edged, stone chippings- as soapstone is a soft natured stone.

claims.text: The Lakdi Pidha gives angular support and cushioning to soapstone pieces in progress and keeps their sharp edges from chipping.

quotes.quote: Provides angular support and cushioning to the under process stone products and prevent their sharp edges from unexpected chippings, during craftsmanship process.

claims.text: In Rajasthan's stone-carving industry, workers and union members describe stone processing as three steps: cutting, carving and polishing.

quotes.quote: Our discussion with the workers and the member of union unfolded that the processing of stone comprises three steps: stone cutting, stone-carving and stone polishing.

claims.text: Locally made machines became prominent in Rajasthan's stone carving after the 2000s, and from 2005 almost every other firm used cheaper Chinese machinery.

quotes.quote: The introduction of locally made machines in the process of stone-carving became prominent after 2000s, however in and after 2005, almost every other firm started using Chinese machinery because of lower costs associated with the latter.

claims.text: A Patharkatti craftsman said hammers and chisels are the main tools, and a product takes anywhere between a day and six months.

quotes.quote: Depending on the object and raw materials used, it can take anywhere between a day to six months to prepare the product. Hammers and chisels are the main tools used to make the product.

claims.text: A Patharkatti craftsman said the stone need not be coloured black, because it turns black by itself once oil and wax are rubbed on it.

quotes.quote: The best part is that one need not colour the product black. It will automatically turn black once oil and wax is rubbed on it.

claims.text: Because their subject is divine, Rajasthan's sculptors of deity images are required to follow the Shilpa Shastra, an ancient Hindu treatise on sculpture and architecture.

quotes.quote: As the subject matter of these images is divine, the sculptors are required to work according to the guidelines laid down in the Shilpa Shastra, an ancient Hindu treatise on sculpture and architecture.

claims.text: In the sthapati tradition, carvers cut along lines and forms marked on the stone by more competent sculptors, which needs great skill and years of experience.

quotes.quote: The carvers carve on the stone following the lines and forms marked out on the stone by the more competent sculptors. Superficially, this may seem mechanical, but it requires great skill and years of experience.

claims.text: In the chiselling of the eye, netron meelanam, the chief sthapati opens the eye of the deity image before its installation.

quotes.quote: Another puja of great importance is the "chiselling of the eye" or netron meelanam. This means opening the eye of the God, in idol form, preceding installation. This is attended to by the project's chief sthapati.

claims.text: Soapstone is a metamorphic rock whose composition includes talc, mica, chlorite, carbonate and amphibole, and its high talc content makes it soft and craft-friendly.

quotes.quote: Soapstone is a metamorphic rockxii. Chemical composition of soapstone includes talk, mica, chlorite, carbonate, amphibole and other natural minerals.
Due to higher amount of talk, as its basic composition, soapstone displays, soft and craft-friendly behaviorxiii.

claims.text: The Dhakotha study describes soapstone as non-porous, non-absorbent, a low conductor of electricity, heat resistant and resistant to acid and alkaline substances.

quotes.quote: Among physical qualities, soapstone is a- nonporous, nonabsorbent, low conductor of electricity, heat resistant, higher specific heat capacity, resistant to acid and alkaline substances.

claims.text: Dhakotha's craftsmen use blackish grey, pink, orange, light green and dark green soapstone.

quotes.quote: In Dhakotha craft clustersxiv, blackish grey, pink, orange, light green and dark green colored soapstone are used for craftsmanship purposes.

claims.text: Several soapstone mines around Dhakotha in Kendujhar district make the cluster self-dependent for a continuous supply of raw material.

quotes.quote: As, there are several soapstone mines available around Dhakotha area, which is situated in Kendujhar districtxv, so, this feature makes Dhakotha craft cluster, selfdependent regarding continuous raw material availability.

claims.text: The geologically old land of Rajasthan, rich in hard rocks such as granites, marbles, quartzite and slates, has been a stone-carver's paradise.

quotes.quote: The geologically old land of Rajasthan, rich in different kinds of hard rocks like granites, marbles, quartzite, slates, and other metamorphic rocks, has been a stone-carver's paradise.

claims.text: The marble of the Taj Mahal was mined at the famous Makrana quarries, which also supplied the Dilwara Jain temples at Mount Abu.

quotes.quote: The quarries at Makrana are quite famous, for it is from these quarries that the marble used in the Taj Mahal was mined. Also built using marble from Makrana mines were the exquisite Dilwara Jain temples at Mt Abu.

claims.text: Rupbas, near Agra, and Karauli still produce the red sandstone the Mughals used for their forts and palaces at Agra, Delhi and Fatehpur Sikri.

quotes.quote: Rupbas (near Agra) and Karauli still produce the red sandstone that was used by the Mughals to build their forts and palaces at Agra, Delhi, and Fatehpur Sikri.

claims.text: Barmer produces yellow marble for delicate carvings and Ajmer produces granites, according to Haryana's culture department.

quotes.quote: Barmer produces yellow marble for delicate carvings, and Ajmer produces granites.

claims.text: In Jaipur white marble is carved into statues of gods and goddesses and animal and human figures, and artisans create marble images of the deities as well as domestic utensils such as bowls for grinding spices.

quotes.quote: In Jaipur, white marble is used for carving out statues of gods and goddesses as well as animal and human figures.
Here one can see artisans creating marble images of the deities as well as domestic utensils such as bowls for grinding spices and kneading dough.

claims.text: The soft stone quarried at Dungarpur, used by Rajasthan's carvers for images of deities, turns black when oiled.

quotes.quote: The soft chromatic stone mined from the quarries of Dungarpur are used by the stone carvers of the state for carving images of the deities. The stone becomes black when oiled.
Dungarpur has a soft shaded stone which turns black when oiled and is used for icon-making.

claims.text: The green-spotted, copper-coloured tamra stone found in Sawai Madhopur is used for making images.

quotes.quote: The green-spotted copper coloured tamra stone found in Sawaimadhopur is used in making images.

claims.text: A very pliable soft stone from Bhilwara is used as a substitute for alabaster.

quotes.quote: A soft stone in Bhilwara is very pliable and it is used as a substitute for alabaster.

claims.text: Asia InCH names yellow limestone, sandstone, and coloured and white marble as the main stones of Rajasthan's stone-carving areas.

quotes.quote: The main stone found here is the yellow lime stone, sand stone, and coloured and white marble.

claims.text: Jaisalmer's famous yellow sandstone is found in areas surrounding the city and comes from mines such as Jethwai, Cipla and Moolsagar.

quotes.quote: The famous yellow sandstone of Jaisalmer is found in areas surrounding the city. It comes from mines like Jethwai, Cipla and Moolsagar.

claims.text: Makrana marble is a calcite marble from the Makrana and Parbatsar tehsils of Nagaur district in Rajasthan.

quotes.locator: Results, Characterization of the Makrana marbles
quotes.quote: Makrana marble is calcite marble from the Makrana and Parbatsar Tehsils of Nagaur District of Rajasthan, in India.

claims.text: White Makrana marble has interlocking recrystallized calcite grains that give it a high polish and excellent compressive strength.

quotes.quote: White Makrana marble is distinguished by its interlocking recrystallized calcite grains, which provide a high polish and excellent compressive strength.

claims.text: The Makrana marble samples studied had a bulk specific gravity of 2.7 and compressive strength from 60 MPa to 75 MPa.

quotes.locator: Results, Characterization of the Makrana marbles
quotes.quote: The bulk specific gravity was found to be 2.7, and compressive strength ranged from 60 MPa to 75 MPa.

Granite, sandstone and schist are the dominant stones of Pakistan and India, while white marble is carved at Jaipur, hard black granite at Patharkatti and soapstone at Dhakotha.

sentences.text: Guilds of masons and stone carvers have existed in India since the 7th century BC, according to Haryana's culture department, and the skills were handed down as family lore from father to son.
Stone carving in Bihar reached its zenith in the Mauryan period, whose finest examples are the rock-cut caves of the Barabar and Nagarjuni Hills in Jahanabad district.

India Currents writes that Gujarat's stonework evolved dramatically under Solanki rule (942-1304) and during the Sultanate reign (1403-1573), and in the Solanki period Jain temples stood apart from Hindu ones by heavy use of marble.
Gujarat's Sultanate rulers built mosques and tombs on Islamic principles but engaged local stone craftsmen, long masters of Hindu and Jain temple architecture, for the embellishments.

Sources differ on when Patharkatti's carvers came: Folkartopedia says Gaud Brahmins built the Vishnupad Temple some 400 years ago, the Free Press Journal that Queen Ahilyabai Holkar brought craftsmen from Rajasthan in 1787, and a craftsman that his Jaipur ancestors were employed for the temple work in 1787.

The Free Press Journal calls it a 300-year-old craft, while The Better India dates the Vishnupada temple to the 8th century, says Ahilyabai only played a small role in the migration, and quotes the UMSAS director that black-stone sculptures in Bihar are much older than the temple.
In the 1960s Upendra Maharathi Shilp Anusandhan Sansthan started a training centre at Patharkatti to bring other communities into a craft limited to Gaud Brahmins.
The 2010-2011 Dhakotha study describes soapstone carving there as a comparatively new craft with around 55-60 years of existence.
In stone carving generally, Rockwell calls the point chisel the workhorse of carving, cutting away at least 85% of the stone removed in carving a statue.

Sources differ on machines: The Art of Making in Antiquity essay says granite carvers in India still use the same basic range of tools as their predecessors and mechanised tools are still only used sparsely, while a Rajasthan study says almost every other firm started using Chinese machinery in and after 2005.
The same essay says metal carving tools need continual sharpening, and that in India teams of twenty carvers are routinely accompanied by as many as three blacksmiths.

At Dhakotha, soapstone carving is shown in 12 stages, among them rough cutting with chisel and hammer, edge cutting with an electric stone cutter, drawing the design, etching its lines, chiselling, fine carving and sanding.
Dhakotha's carvers commonly use chisels with many cutting-tip shapes, hammers, mallets, filers, a Lakdi Pidha support and a Jute Chatti cushion.
In Jaisalmer a design traced on butter paper guides the artisan, the form is often carved with an electric tool, and the finer detailing is done with diamond-tipped chisels.
Asia InCH lists hammers, thin, thick and fine chisels, a brush and a metal stencil among the tools of Jaisalmer's stone carving.
Soapstone is a metamorphic rock whose high talc content makes it soft and craft-friendly, and Dhakotha's craftsmen use blackish grey, pink, orange, light green and dark green soapstone.
Makrana marble, a calcite marble from Nagaur district of Rajasthan, was mined for the Taj Mahal and is a highly prized ornamental and masonry stone.
Rupbas and Karauli still produce the red sandstone used by the Mughals, while Jaisalmer's famous yellow sandstone comes from mines around the city.
The soft stone of Dungarpur turns black when oiled, and a Patharkatti craftsman said his stone turns black once oil and wax are rubbed on it.
The specialty of Patharkatti's artisans is hard black granite, though they also work on marble, sandstone and palewa.
Rajasthan is a geologically old land rich in hard rocks such as granites, marbles, quartzite and slates.
White Makrana marble has interlocking recrystallized calcite grains that give it a high polish.
One part of a study gives fresh Makrana marble an open porosity of 0.1-0.3%, another part 0.2% to 0.5%.
Undulation and pitting on the marble floors of the Taj Mahal and Jaswant Thada are attributed to tourist activity, acid rain and air pollution.
Rajasthan continues to be one of the major centres of stone carving in India, according to Haryana's culture department, and Jaipur is the state's centre of marble carving.
Stone carving is practised widely in Jaisalmer, and Pindwara in Sirohi district is called the main hub of India's temple-building industry.
Patharkatti in Gaya district is one of the major centres of stone craft in Bihar, and Bihar Tourism names Nalanda, Kaimur and Patna as the other centres.
Dhakotha, a village in Kendujhar district of Odisha on the bank of the Baitarini River, has several soapstone mines around it.
India Currents writes that stone carving is still a vibrant profession in Gujarat because temple building has never ceased there.
Rajasthan's stone carvers are noted for jali, or latticework, and jali screens of sandstone and marble let women in purdah watch the court without being seen.
Jaisalmer's carvers make overhangs or chhajja, windows or jharokha, lattice screens and household items such as the chakla.
Rajasthan's sculptors of deity images are required to follow the Shilpa Shastra, an ancient Hindu treatise on sculpture and architecture.
In the shilpa tradition Himalayan Academy describes, stones are classed by their sound as male, female or neuter, and the Shastras prescribe male stones for male images.
Pattharkatti's artisans transform rough black granite into statues, and the kharal, an oblong boat-shaped stone vessel, is used to prepare medicines and masalas.
Silicosis is caused by long-term inhalation of inorganic dust with high concentrations of free crystalline silica.
The authors of a western Rajasthan sculpting study write that motorized carving instruments generate excessive dust in a short time, and none of the sculpting units in that study used wet drilling.
Of 114 silicosis patients from those sculpting units, with data collected from January 2021 to April 2023, 109 used no personal protective equipment at work.
Health camps held in Pindwara since 2016 found silicosis in 35% of the screened workers, and the median age of those diagnosed was just 34 years.
Silicosis has no cure and prevention is the only option, and ventilation, wet drilling, dust control equipment and respirators are recommended to cut exposure to silica dust.
